doc.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Miles Davis band and Kind of Blue
title: Miles needling Bill Evans
summary: Cobb says Miles teased people and tells of the remark in the car in Ohio.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: A lot is made of the issue of race among musicians and particularly – not particularly – but how Miles related to Bill Evans, sort of needling him. What do you think was behind that?
Needling. Would needle, so to speak, Bill Evans.

He was – that was the way he was. He would do that to a lot of people. He would say things just to see what your reaction could be. He used to bounce – liked to bounce things off of people to see what would come back.
Whether it was race or not.

Whether it was race or anything. He said something in the car one time. We were sitting out in Ohio. We were just sitting, waiting to check in a hotel or something. We’re just sitting there. So him and Cannon – we were all sitting in the car – him and Cannon was talking about something. Whatever it was, Bill went to say something, and Miles said, “Wait a minute, man. We don’t want no white opinions.” But Bill – he was kidding, but Bill didn’t know how to take that. So he would say things like that. Then he would say things like, “You know, man, when a new guy comes in the band, he has to make love to everybody.” Bill didn’t know how to take that either. But it’s just needle. That’s what it is. Because he was like that.
Yeah, he would just see how it rolls off you. It’s funny when I think about it.
What was – could you cut the air at that moment?

No – well, yeah. You could see Bill was thinking about it. He’s saying, now wait a minute, what’s going on here? Then another thing was going on at the time. We used to go to all these places that they used to – the band used to play when Joe and Red and Paul was there. They go back to
these places and see Bill sitting there. Say, whoa, wait a minute. Something’s wrong with this picture. “What’s going on, Miles?”

Yeah. That didn’t lay on Bill that – he didn’t – say, wait a minute. He felt shaky. He was in a whole different atmosphere. But they got – a little later, they got used to seeing him there, after they heard him play.

We’re still, even today, negotiating these sensitivities: what you can say, what you can’t say, how people are going to process it. Just the thing that happened with this lady [Sheira?] in trying to tell a story of reconciliation and how she actually felt about something.
Yeah, and they chopped it down to where they make it sound the way they wanted to make it sound.

I almost feel that same when I read these stories. What you’re repeating is something that’s in a bunch of texts. How people read this has a lot to do with how we have come to grips, or even to understand the complexity of it. Not to – I don’t think in either case was it – Bill Evans had to manage some stuff, Miles had to manage his stuff, you, as bandmembers, had to manage the stuff, and the audience is managing stuff. It’s just not so simple.
Yeah, there’s some mean stuff goes on a lot of times. Like you say, you have to manage it, though. That’s what I’ve probably been doing all my life: managing stuff.
